text: Several adjacent tennis courts together stand in for a map of the world.
Each player represents a nuclear-armed bloc of nations, called a combatant.
A tennis ball lobbed with a racquet onto the map represents one thermonuclear warhead.
Each ball carries a nominal yield of 5 megatons.
A game master uses a computer to tally the results through statistical indices.
Only the map counts as territory: a ball affects the map, never the physical court or
players.
Players fix one profile, PEAK or CURRENT, before play and use it for every country.
A bloc's ball allotment equals the sum of its members' BALLS under the chosen profile.
A ball strikes a country only if its first bounce lands inside that country's zone
circle.
A member may target a zone whose centre lies within REACH x 12.5 m of its own centre;
REACH 4 is unlimited.
A member with SECOND_STRIKE true may launch its remaining balls after its own zone is
struck; others may not.
A bloc may spend one CBW token per turn to cancel one ball of a targeted bloc, then
loses 1 RESTRAINT.
When the game master's tally is tied, the bloc with the higher mean RESTRAINT wins the
tie.
Zones are placed at the post-nudge x_m and y_m positions listed in the ledger.
A country marked UNRETRIEVED plays with every derived stat at the value its null
fields give (zero).
Bloc members do not fight each other; NONALIGN is a pool, so its members act as
separate one-country blocs.
Under CURRENT, each sharing host holds STAGED of its provider's balls. They stay in
the bloc total, launch from the host's zone with the provider's REACH, and are lost if
the host's zone is struck before they launch.
A bloc with no balls is still a combatant: it plays CBW tokens only and takes part in
the tally and tie-breaks.
A bloc's CBW stock is the sum of its members' CBW_TOKENS, capped at 12; NONALIGN
members are one-country blocs, each holding its own tokens (at most 6).

countries.name: Albania

final_titles: Albania and weapons of mass destruction

summary: No nuclear weapons program is described. The article only notes an alleged 1960s
intelligence attempt to buy atomic-bomb information in Italy.
The article documents no biological weapons program.
Albania declared a chemical stockpile found in a bunker in 2002. Its origin is
undocumented and possibly Chinese. The OPCW confirmed complete destruction in July
The article documents no radiological weapons program.

note: No national warhead figure in the article.

attribution: Albania's CWC declaration, as reported in the article (16,678 kg)

event: Accedes to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
Accedes to the Biological Weapons Convention.
Among the first signatories of the Chemical Weapons Convention.
About 600 bulk chemical containers found in an abandoned bunker.
Declares its chemical stockpile; deposits CTBT accession.
OPCW confirms Albania is first state to destroy its entire chemical arsenal under the
CWC.

disputed_claims: Origin of the chemical stockpile (possibly China, mid-1970s) is undocumented
speculation.
A 1960s Sigurimi effort to buy atomic-bomb information via an agent in Italy is
reported only from a TV documentary.
narrative: Albania's weapons-of-mass-destruction story is almost entirely a chemical one. In late
2002 about six hundred bulk chemical containers were found in a disused bunker, and
the next spring Albania declared them under the Chemical Weapons Convention, becoming
one of only a handful of states ever to declare a stockpile. The cache, roughly 16.7
tonnes, held blister agents such as mustard and lewisite along with irritant
compounds. Its origin is unclear: the article suggests it may have come from China
under Enver Hoxha in the 1970s, but stresses that no records were found and that the
idea is speculation. With United States funding through the Nunn-Lugar Cooperative
Threat Reduction program, at a cost of about 48 million dollars, the material was
eliminated, and in July 2007 the OPCW confirmed Albania as the first state to destroy
its entire declared chemical arsenal under the treaty. On the nuclear side the article
records only a reported 1960s intelligence episode in which Albanian operatives in
Italy were offered, for a fee, information supposedly linked to French atomic
research; nothing suggests a weapons program followed. Albania is a party to the NPT,
the BWC and the CTBT, and joined the Geneva Protocol in 1989.

bloc_justification: Sino-Albanian alliance after leaving the Warsaw Pact (1961-78).

countries.name: Algeria

final_titles: Algeria and weapons of mass destruction

summary: A nuclear program began in 1981 with Argentine, then Chinese, help. Algeria denies any
military aim and its reactors are under IAEA safeguards. Some intelligence assessments
alleged weapons intent; the article is sceptical.
The article documents no biological weapons program.
The article documents no chemical weapons program.
The article documents no radiological weapons program.

note: No national warhead figure in the article.

event: Nuclear program launched with Argentine cooperation, later Chinese.
Army signs agreement with China for a research reactor, later named Es-Salam.
US reveals the reactor; Algeria denies military purpose and accepts IAEA safeguards.
Joins the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
Accedes to the Biological Weapons Convention.
Signs the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.

disputed_claims: A 1998 assessment attributed to Spain's intelligence service alleged weapons intent;
Algeria denies it.
1991 US press claims of Chinese help toward a bomb were not borne out, per the
article.
narrative: Algeria launched a nuclear program in 1981, working first with Argentina and later
with China. In 1991 the United States said it had uncovered details of a reactor being
built at Ain Oussera, and a Washington newspaper accused Algeria of pursuing a bomb
with Chinese help. Algiers acknowledged the reactor, a Chinese-supplied research unit
named Es-Salam, meaning peace, but denied any secrecy or military intent, and US
satellite imagery reportedly pointed the same way. Algeria placed the reactor under
IAEA safeguards in November 1991, and a second, smaller research reactor acquired in
1989 is also monitored by the agency. Suspicion lingered: a 1998 assessment attributed
to Spain's National Intelligence Centre is cited as saying Algeria intended to produce
weapons-usable material, and analysts noted that the larger reactor could in principle
be diverted. The article itself is sceptical, observing that repeatedly forecast dates
for an Algerian bomb have passed without one appearing and without the IAEA voicing
doubts. On treaties, Algeria joined the NPT in 1995, has ratified the CWC, acceded to
the BWC in 2001, and signed the TPNW in 2017 without ratifying it as of 2022. No
biological, chemical or radiological program is documented, and talk of a civilian
power plant had produced no project by 2022.

countries.name: Argentina

final_titles: Argentina and weapons of mass destruction

summary: The military regime ran nuclear weapons research in the early 1980s. It was abandoned
after democracy returned in December 1983. No weapon was built or tested.
The article documents no biological weapons program.
The article documents no chemical weapons program.
The article documents no radiological weapons program.

note: No national warhead figure in the article.

event: Accedes to the Geneva Protocol.
Ratifies the Biological Weapons Convention.
After the Falklands War, US intelligence judges Argentina able to build a bomb.
Officials disclose an enrichment capability; civilian rule returns and the program
ends.
Condor 2 missile project reportedly scrapped under US pressure and budget limits.
Mendoza Declaration and the ABACC inspection agreement with Brazil.
Accedes to the NPT and ratifies the Chemical Weapons Convention.

narrative: Argentina's flirtation with nuclear weapons belongs to the military regime of 1976 to
1983. The article describes a weapons research effort in the early 1980s, spurred
partly by a parallel Brazilian program, and notes that after the 1982 Falklands War US
intelligence judged Argentina capable of building a bomb from its civilian nuclear
base. In November 1983 officials disclosed that research at the Balseiro Institute had
produced a domestic enrichment capability. Within weeks democracy returned and
President Raul Alfonsin put the nuclear sector back under civilian control; the
program was dropped, helped by the lack of real hostility with Brazil and by Brazil's
greater resources in any arms race. The 1980s also saw the Alacran and Condor missile
projects. The Condor 2, a design of roughly 1,000 km meant to be developed with
Egyptian and Iraqi help, drew condemnation from the United States and the Missile
Technology Control Regime and was cancelled around 1990 under President Menem.
Argentina then turned firmly to nonproliferation: mutual inspections with Brazil
through ABACC from 1991, the 1991 Mendoza Declaration renouncing chemical and
biological arms, NPT accession in 1995, and ratification of the BWC in 1979 and the
CWC in 1995. A lesser-known episode is that in the early 1960s Argentina sold about 90
tons of unsafeguarded uranium concentrate to Israel.

bloc_justification: Tlatelolco zone; nuclear rival-partner of Brazil.
Tlatelolco zone; ABACC partner of Brazil.

countries.name: Australia

final_titles: Australia and weapons of mass destruction

summary: Governments explored acquiring British or US weapons from 1956 and funded enrichment
research into the mid-1980s. No weapons were obtained. Australia hosted British atomic
tests in 1952-57.
A defence subcommittee studied biological warfare from 1947, including offensive
potential. Activity was scaled back in the early 1950s.
Australia held British and US chemical munitions in the Second World War and trialled
them but never used or produced them. Stocks were destroyed or dumped at sea after the
war.
The article documents no radiological weapons program.

note: No national warhead figure in the article.

event: Virologist Macfarlane Burnet joins a chemical and biological warfare subcommittee.
First British atomic test at the Monte Bello Islands.
Air minister recommends acquiring tactical nuclear weapons for RAAF aircraft.
Ratifies the NPT, signed in 1970.
Ratifies the Biological Weapons Convention.
Ratifies the Chemical Weapons Convention via domestic legislation.

disputed_claims: Total chemical munitions dumped at sea is given as about 21,030 tons with no reference
year.
narrative: Australia holds no weapons of mass destruction, yet its record touches research or
stockpiling in all three classic categories. During the Second World War it ran
extensive chemical-weapons trials and held British and American stocks, including
mustard, phosgene and lewisite, some of which were shipped to New Guinea for possible
use against Japanese tunnel positions but never used. After the war most of the stock
was burned, vented or dumped at sea off Brisbane, Sydney and Melbourne, a total the
article puts at about 21,000 tons, and stray caches kept turning up for decades. From
1947 a defence subcommittee advised by the virologist Macfarlane Burnet studied
biological warfare, including the offensive potential of agents against regional food
supplies, before the effort was wound down in the early 1950s as Prime Minister
Menzies turned his attention to nuclear arms. Nuclear interest ran longer. From 1956
ministers and air force chiefs explored acquiring British or American tactical
weapons, Australia hosted British atomic tests at Monte Bello, Emu Field and Maralinga
between 1952 and 1957, and domestic enrichment research continued until it lost
funding in the mid-1980s. Even so, Australia signed the NPT in 1970 and ratified it in
1973, ratified the BWC in 1977 and the CWC in 1994, and chairs the Australia Group
export-control forum. Lowy Institute polling cited in the article shows rising but
still minority public support for acquiring nuclear weapons.

bloc_justification: ANZUS treaty ally of the United States.
ANZUS treaty ally of the United States.

countries.name: Belarus

final_titles: Belarus and weapons of mass destruction

summary: Belarus inherited Soviet nuclear weapons in 1991 and returned them to Russia by
November 1996. Since 2023 Russia says it has stationed non-strategic weapons there
under Russian control.
No Belarusian national program is described. A Minsk institute reportedly supported
the Soviet program in the 1980s; that activity is recorded under RUS.
No Belarusian national program is described beyond its status as a Soviet republic
during the Soviet chemical program.
The article documents no radiological weapons program.

note: No national warheads. Lukashenko claimed in Dec 2024 to host 'dozens' of Russian
warheads; unverified as of 2025.

hosted_warheads.note: Lukashenko claimed 'dozens' (Dec 2024); no open-source confirmation as of 2025.

event: Signs the Lisbon Protocol with Kazakhstan and Ukraine, joining START.
Budapest Memorandum gives security assurances in exchange for denuclearization.
Withdrawal of ex-Soviet nuclear weapons completed in November.
Referendum lifts constitutional ban on hosting nuclear weapons and drops neutrality.
Russia supplies nuclear-capable Iskander-M missiles; Putin says warheads arrived in
June.
Belarus exercises nuclear-capable Iskanders and Su-25s with training warheads.

disputed_claims: Presence of Russian warheads in Belarus is claimed but not confirmed by open sources
Operational control: Lukashenko implies Belarusian say; Putin says Russia keeps
control.
narrative: Belarus entered independence in 1991 holding part of the Soviet nuclear arsenal,
chiefly mobile intercontinental missiles based near Lida and Mazyr according to US
think-tank studies. Through the 1992 Lisbon Protocol it joined the START treaty and
committed to the NPT as a non-nuclear state, renounced the inherited weapons without
preconditions, becoming the first post-Soviet state to do so, and received security
assurances in the 1994 Budapest Memorandum. With help from the US Cooperative Threat
Reduction program the last weapons left in November 1996. The story reversed after
Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. A February 2022 referendum removed the
constitutional ban on hosting nuclear arms along with Belarus's neutral status, and
Moscow and Minsk agreed to station Russian non-strategic weapons. Russia supplied
nuclear-capable Iskander-M short-range missiles and modified Belarusian Su-25 jets to
carry nuclear bombs, and Putin said warheads began arriving in June 2023. As of 2025
open sources had found no conclusive proof that warheads are actually stored in the
country, though Lukashenko claimed in December 2024 that it hosts dozens; Putin
insists Russia keeps control, and Moscow has floated basing an intermediate-range
Oreshnik missile there. Belarus ratified the CWC in 1996 and, as a Soviet republic,
was covered when the USSR ratified the BWC. A Minsk research institute reportedly
helped import virus samples for the Soviet biological program in the early 1980s.

bloc_justification: CSTO member and Union State partner of Russia.

countries.name: Belgium

final_titles: Belgium and weapons of mass destruction

summary: Belgium has no national nuclear weapons program. It has hosted US weapons under NATO
nuclear sharing since 1963.
The article documents no biological weapons program.
No Belgian program is described. Belgian territory was a major chemical battlefield in
the First World War.
The article documents no radiological weapons program.

note: No national warheads. Hosts an estimated 10-15 US B61 bombs (Kristensen et al., 2023).

hosted_warheads.attribution: Belgium article, citing Kristensen et al. 2023 (low end of 10-15)
hosted_warheads.note: US B61 bombs at Kleine Brogel.

event: United States begins stationing nuclear weapons in Belgium.
Ratifies the Biological Weapons Convention.
US ground-launched cruise missile wing deploys at Florennes.
Cruise missiles removed under the INF Treaty.
Ratifies the Chemical Weapons Convention.
Parliament narrowly rejects a resolution to remove US nuclear weapons, 66 to 74.

narrative: Belgium has never pursued weapons of mass destruction of its own, but it has hosted
American nuclear weapons since 1963 under NATO nuclear sharing. Open-source estimates
cited in the article put the current holding at roughly 10 to 15 US B61 gravity bombs
at Kleine Brogel Air Base, kept in US custody by a USAFE munitions support squadron
and earmarked for the Belgian F-16s of the 10th Tactical Wing. From 1984 Belgium also
hosted a US ground-launched cruise missile wing at Florennes; the missiles were
withdrawn under the 1987 INF Treaty, the last leaving in December 1988. Domestic
politics have pushed back at times. In January 2020 a parliamentary resolution calling
for removal of the US weapons failed by 66 votes to 74, a debate sharpened by the
Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which no NATO member has signed.
Belgium's earlier encounter with weapons of mass destruction was as a battlefield
rather than a possessor: during the First World War its territory saw heavy use of
chlorine, phosgene and mustard gas by both the Entente powers and the German Empire.
Belgium signed the BWC in 1972 and ratified it in 1979, and signed the CWC in 1993 and
ratified it in 1997. For Eschaton purposes it is a host state: it brings delivery
aircraft and basing to its bloc but no warheads of its own.

bloc_justification: NATO founding member and nuclear-sharing host.

countries.name: Brazil

final_titles: Brazil and weapons of mass destruction

summary: The military regime ran a covert 'Parallel Program' toward a weapons option in the
1970s-80s. It was exposed and dismantled in 1990. Brazil is described as
nuclear-latent.
The article documents no biological weapons program.
The article documents no chemical weapons program.
The article documents no radiological weapons program.

note: No national warhead figure in the article.

event: Signs the Treaty of Tlatelolco on a Latin American nuclear-weapon-free zone.
Ratifies the Biological Weapons Convention.
President Sarney announces a domestic uranium enrichment capability.
President Collor symbolically seals the Cachimbo test shaft and exposes the program.
Ends nuclear rivalry with Argentina; ABACC and full-scope IAEA safeguards follow.
Accedes to the NPT.
Signs but does not ratify the TPNW.

disputed_claims: A cited Los Alamos assessment holds Brazil could build a weapon within about three
years of deciding to.
narrative: Under military rule in the 1970s and 1980s Brazil ran a secret effort, the so-called
Parallel Program, aimed at a nuclear weapons option. It grew out of rivalry with
Argentina and drew on West German nuclear technology supplied without IAEA safeguards,
and the article reports that Brazil also sought enriched uranium from China in the
early 1980s. In 1987 President Jose Sarney announced a domestic enrichment capability.
After civilian rule returned, President Fernando Collor de Mello publicly closed the
Cachimbo test shaft in 1990, symbolically shovelling it shut, and exposed the effort.
A congressional inquiry then uncovered secret bank accounts code-named Delta and found
that the military had designed bomb devices and had covertly sent uranium to Iraq in
1981. In 1991 Brazil and Argentina ended their nuclear competition, creating the ABACC
inspection agency and accepting full-scope IAEA safeguards. The 1988 constitution
limits nuclear activity to peaceful purposes, and Brazil acceded to the NPT in 1998,
one of the last states to do so, having ratified the BWC in 1973; it ratified the CWC
in 1996 and signed the TPNW in 2017 without ratifying it. Brazil is widely described
as nuclear-latent: its enrichment plants and naval nuclear-propulsion program mean it
retains the know-how, and one assessment cited in the article puts a weapon within
about three years of a decision. US officials, including Colin Powell in 2004, have
said they see no Brazilian intent to build one.

bloc_justification: Tlatelolco zone; nuclear rival-partner of Argentina.
Tlatelolco zone; ABACC partner of Argentina.

countries.name: Bulgaria

final_titles: Bulgaria and weapons of mass destruction

summary: Bulgaria never developed nuclear weapons. Its Soviet-era missiles were prepared to
launch Soviet warheads in wartime; an alleged warhead facility is disputed.
The article documents no biological weapons program.
Bulgaria produced chemical weapons, centred near Smyadovo, with few public details. It
ratified the CWC in 1994, began dismantlement in 2000 and holds no WMD as of 2025.
The article documents no radiological weapons program.

note: No national warhead figure in the article.

event: First missile brigade formed.
Alleged Soviet-Bulgarian warhead unit disbanded, per a disputed account.
Nuclear missile launch pads and equipment dismantled.
Ratifies the Chemical Weapons Convention.
Begins chemical weapons dismantlement.
All Scud, Frog and Oka missiles destroyed under a deal with the US.
Highly enriched research-reactor fuel airlifted back to Russia with IAEA monitoring.

disputed_claims: An anonymous Soviet officer alleged a joint facility held about 70 tactical warheads
until 1989; a Russian official denied it.
Bulgaria's foreign ministry denied in 2001 that any nuclear weapons were present.
narrative: Bulgaria's history with weapons of mass destruction is mostly about chemicals and
about Soviet nuclear planning. The only known chemical weapons production site was
near Smyadovo and now makes civilian chemicals; details of the program are scarce, but
Bulgaria ratified the CWC in 1994, began dismantling in 2000, and as of 2025 is
described as holding no weapons of mass destruction. Bulgaria never built nuclear
weapons. During the Cold War its army fielded Soviet-supplied Scud, Frog and Oka
missiles whose launchers were prepared to fire Soviet warheads, which Moscow planned
to bring in quickly if war with NATO broke out. The nuclear launch equipment was
dismantled in 1991 and the missiles themselves were destroyed in 2002 under an
agreement with the United States; today's short-range missiles carry conventional
warheads. In the 1980s several Bulgarian air force officers trained in the Soviet
Union on dropping nuclear bombs from MiG-23 aircraft. A mid-1990s press investigation,
based on an anonymous Soviet officer's account, alleged a secret joint facility that
had held around 70 tactical warheads until 1989; another Russian official denied the
story, and in 2001 Bulgaria's foreign ministry denied that any nuclear weapons were
present. In 2003 the IAEA helped return highly enriched research-reactor fuel to
Russia. Bulgaria has signed and ratified the BWC, and in 2018 commentators floated it
as a possible new location for US weapons then stationed in Turkey.

countries.name: Canada

final_titles: Canada and weapons of mass destruction

summary: Never had its own weapons. It contributed to the Manhattan Project and hosted US
weapons from 1963 to 1984 under NATO and NORAD.
An offensive and defensive research program centred on Suffield; Canada says all
stockpiles are destroyed. Dates 1946-56 are from the root WMD article.
A major Allied producer in both world wars, with combat use in the first. Human
testing continued into the early 1970s; lethal agents were later abandoned and
destroyed.
The article documents no radiological weapons program.

note: No national warheads. Hosted 250-450 US warheads on its bases in 1963-72; none since

event: Canada joins the Tube Alloys committee; hosts the Montreal Laboratory.
First US nuclear bombs on Canadian soil, at Goose Bay; one dropped in the St Lawrence.
US nuclear weapons deployed for Canadian forces (Bomarc, Genie, CF-104, Honest John).
Ratifies the NPT; Honest John retired.
Ratifies the BWC; Bomarc phased out.
Approves US cruise missile testing in Alberta, sparking protest.
Last US nuclear weapons (Genie) leave Canada.
Review committee begins inspections to verify defensive-only CBW work.
Ratifies the CWC (26 September).

use_history.conflict: World War I (Allied chemical weapons; year not given)

disputed_claims: Warheads for the CF-104 squadrons are estimated at 90-210; open sources are lacking.
Total US warheads on Canadian bases in 1963-72 is given as a range, 250 to 450.
narrative: Canada has never possessed weapons of mass destruction of its own, yet it was deeply
involved in all three kinds. In nuclear matters it was a junior partner from the
start: under the 1942-43 arrangements it joined the Tube Alloys effort, hosted the
Montreal Laboratory and supplied uranium ore and at least one Los Alamos scientist to
the Manhattan Project, and it went on supplying fissile material to allies through the
Cold War while choosing not to build a bomb. US bombs first came onto Canadian soil in
1950, when Strategic Air Command stationed 11 atomic bombs at Goose Bay in Labrador;
one was jettisoned and its conventional explosives detonated over the St Lawrence
River. From 1963 to 1984 Canada took part in NATO's nuclear mission with four
US-supplied systems, Bomarc air-defence missiles, Honest John rockets in Germany,
CF-104 strike aircraft in Europe and Genie air-to-air rockets on CF-101 interceptors,
all with warheads in US custody; between 250 and 450 warheads were on Canadian bases
until 1972, and the Genie remained until 1984. US weapons were also stored at Argentia
in Newfoundland from 1968 to 1994. Canada ratified the NPT in 1970, remains under the
NATO nuclear umbrella, and opposes the TPNW, the one disarmament treaty it has not
joined. Canada was also a major Allied producer and developer of chemical weapons in
both world wars, using them in combat in the first. At Suffield, thousands of Canadian
soldiers were exposed to mustard and other agents in wartime tests, and human testing
with nerve agents continued into the early 1970s; munitions were dumped at sea off
Nova Scotia after both wars. Its biological research program, run with Britain and the
United States, studied offensive as well as defensive uses. Canada says all stockpiles
are destroyed, and a review committee has inspected its defensive work since 1990. It
ratified the BWC in 1972 and the CWC in 1995.

countries.name: China

final_titles: China and weapons of mass destruction

summary: Recognised NPT nuclear-weapon state since its 1964 test, with a declared no-first-use
policy. About 620 warheads in 2026 and growing; triad since 2020.
The US State Department says two facilities produced biological agents from the 1950s
to 1987, and some analysts think work continues. China denies any offensive program.
China reportedly declared and destroyed two or three production facilities in 1997.
Information on any current program is very limited; the US alleges non-compliance.
No state program. The article records crude radiological devices tested by Cultural
Revolution rebels in 1967.

note: About 620 (2026). Only NPT state expanding fast; projected 1,000 by 2030. Most
warheads stored apart.

event: Nuclear weapons program begins (15 January).
Soviet Union withdraws all advisers from the program.
First test, '596', at Lop Nur; no-first-use pledge declared.
Project 639, the test seen internationally as China's first H-bomb.
Border war; the Soviet Union weighs a massive nuclear strike on China.
The world's most recent known atmospheric nuclear test.
Deng Xiaoping begins nuclear weapons technology transfers to Pakistan.
Accedes to the Biological Weapons Convention.
Accedes to the NPT.
Last test (29 July); signs but does not ratify the CTBT.
Ratifies the CWC and declares former chemical facilities.
Builds three large missile silo fields; triad in service.
Victory Day parade first displays the full nuclear triad.

disputed_claims: First thermonuclear test: the infobox and body give December 1966; the lead gives
The US alleges a covert test at Lop Nur on 22 June 2020; the CTBTO detected no
explosion.
Chemical and biological programs: alleged by the US, denied by China.
Observers doubt the credibility of no-first-use; parts of the force may be on launch
on warning.
State media called the silo-field construction windmills until 2024.
narrative: China launched its nuclear weapons program in January 1955, a step some scholars tie
to US nuclear threats during the First Taiwan Strait Crisis. Soviet advisers helped
build the early industry until Moscow cut off all help in 1959-60; Chinese scientists
marked the rupture in the codename of their first bomb, '596', tested at Lop Nur in
October 1964. China declared a no-first-use policy the same year, which it still
upholds, and moved from fission to thermonuclear weapons more quickly than any earlier
nuclear power, with full-scale tests in 1966-67. After the 1969 border war, when the
Soviet Union weighed a massive strike on Chinese cities and nuclear sites, Beijing
aimed its early missiles at Soviet as well as American targets. China carried out 45
tests, including in 1980 the world's most recent known atmospheric test, before
stopping in July 1996 and signing, but not ratifying, the CTBT. In the 1980s it
transferred nuclear weapons technology and a bomb design to Pakistan, before acceding
to the NPT in 1992. For decades China kept a small force at low readiness, with
warheads stored apart from missiles. It is now the world's third-largest arsenal and
the only NPT-recognised one expanding rapidly: about 620 warheads in 2026, projected
to reach 1,000 by 2030. Since 2020 it has fielded a full triad of Dongfeng land
missiles, JL-3 submarine missiles and H-6N bombers, built about 350 new silos, and
reportedly moved parts of its force toward launch on warning. The United States
alleges covert testing at Lop Nur, including an event in June 2020 that the CTBT
monitoring network did not detect. China denies holding offensive chemical or
biological weapons. It reportedly declared and destroyed its former chemical
production facilities in 1997, while the US State Department says two facilities
produced biological agents from the 1950s to 1987. China was itself the target of
Japanese chemical and biological attacks in 1937-45, and up to two million abandoned
Japanese chemical munitions remain on its soil.

countries.name: Egypt

final_titles: Egypt and weapons of mass destruction

summary: No dedicated nuclear weapons program is known since 1952. A civil program from 1954
stalled after 1967; Egypt ratified the NPT in 1981.
Signed but has not ratified the BWC. Sadat said before signing that Egypt held
biological weapons 'in the refrigerators'.
Its most developed program, thought to have peaked in the 1960s; used in North Yemen
1963-67. Outside the CWC pending answers on Israel's nuclear arsenal.
The article documents no radiological weapons program.

note: None; no weapons program is documented.

event: Civil nuclear program begins.
Nasser opens the Soviet-supplied ETRR-1 research reactor at Inchass.
First Egyptian gas attack in North Yemen, on Kawma (8 June).
Kitaf gas attack kills about 140; nuclear development halts after the Six-Day War.
Signs the NPT.
Signs the BWC (10 April), never ratified.
Supplies Syria with chemical shells before the October War.
Begins its campaign for a regional nuclear-weapon-free zone.
Ratifies the NPT.
Acquires the ETRR-2 research reactor from Argentina.

use_history.conflict: North Yemen Civil War 1963-67 (phosgene and mustard)

disputed_claims: Egypt denied using gas in Yemen and suggested the injuries came from napalm.
Aviation Week reported Soviet-crewed nuclear Scuds in Egypt in 1973; the article
reports it only.
Whether Egypt still holds chemical or biological weapons is not established in the
article.
Yemen casualty figures vary; about 1,500 deaths is described as a conservative
estimate.
narrative: Egypt is one of the few states to have used chemical weapons since the First World
War, and one of only four that remain outside the Chemical Weapons Convention. Its
chemical program, the most developed of its weapons efforts, is thought to have peaked
in the 1960s, when Egyptian forces intervening in the North Yemen Civil War dropped
phosgene and mustard bombs on royalist forces and villages. The first attack, on the
village of Kawma in June 1963, was crude and is considered experimental; the attacks
grew more frequent from late 1966, and the worst, on Kitaf in January 1967, killed
about 140 people. A conservative estimate puts total deaths at about 1,500. Egypt
denied using gas, blamed napalm, and accused Britain and the United States of
psychological warfare; the Red Cross voiced concern, and Swiss forensic experts
identified halogen-based agents. Egypt later shared the capability: it supplied Syria
with chemical artillery shells in 1973 as a deterrent before the two states launched
the October War. Egypt's stated policy is to stay out of the Chemical Weapons
Convention until questions over Israel's nuclear weapons are answered. On nuclear
matters, Egypt is not known to have run a dedicated weapons program. A civil program
begun in 1954 gained a Soviet-supplied research reactor at Inchass in 1961 but stalled

narrative: Italy is one of two navbox states whose link goes to a nuclear program article (Spain
is the other), and its story is of an ambition repeatedly redirected into alliance
arrangements. Italian physicists such as Enrico Fermi had been at the forefront of
nuclear science, but the 1947 peace treaty barred Italy from building nuclear weapons,
so it pursued a role through NATO. The first US nuclear weapons arrived in September
1955, Honest John and Corporal missiles meant to slow an attack across the Austrian
and Yugoslav borders, followed by Nike Hercules air-defence missiles. In 1959 Italy
secured 30 Jupiter intermediate-range missiles, crewed by an Italian brigade with US
warheads under a dual key; they were withdrawn in 1963 as part of the settlement of
the Cuban Missile Crisis. Italy had also joined a short-lived French-German-Italian
deterrent plan, ended by de Gaulle in 1958, and then backed the NATO Multilateral
Force, converting the cruiser Giuseppe Garibaldi to carry Polaris missiles and
test-firing them in 1962. When Washington dropped the Multilateral Force in 1964,
Italy turned to a national program in the late 1960s, including the Alfa, a two-stage
solid-fuel missile with a planned 1,600 km range; three test launches took place, the
last in April 1976. Cost, shifting politics and US pressure ended the effort, and
Italy ratified the NPT in May 1975. It has remained a host ever since: cruise
missiles, Lance missiles and nuclear artillery were based there in the Cold War, amid
mass protests in the 1980s, and the last US Army weapons left in 1992. An estimated 70
to 90 US B61 bombs were stored at Aviano and Ghedi as of 2015, for US F-16s and
Italian Tornados, which F-35s are replacing. The article does not cover chemical or
biological weapons; the root WMD article records Fascist Italy's use of mustard gas in
Ethiopia in 1935-36.

narrative: The Empire of Japan waged the largest state chemical and biological campaign of the
Second World War, and postwar Japan, the only country attacked with nuclear weapons,
became a non-nuclear state with the means to build them. Its main chemical plant, on
Okunoshima island, produced tear gas and mustard from 1929, and the army used gas
sporadically in China from 1937 and on a large scale from 1938, against Nationalist
and Communist troops; historians say Emperor Hirohito authorised use on 375 occasions
during the 1938 Battle of Wuhan. Fear of Allied retaliation kept gas from being used
against Western forces. Unit 731 and other units in occupied Manchuria and beyond ran
biological research that included lethal experiments on thousands of prisoners, and
dispersed plague, anthrax, glanders, cholera and other diseases over Chinese cities
and villages from 1940 to 1943; an estimated 200,000 to 500,000 people died. Plans to
strike the United States, including a 1945 plague raid on San Diego, were rejected. A
wartime nuclear program, begun at Riken in 1941, never left the laboratory and ended
in July 1945, weeks before the US atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki killed
between 150,000 and 246,000 people. After the war the United States granted Unit 731
scientists immunity in exchange for their data; only the Soviet Khabarovsk trials of
1949 convicted any, and a Japanese court first acknowledged the germ warfare in 2002.
From 1954 to 1972 the US stationed nuclear weapons in Japan, up to 1,300 at the peak
and mostly on Okinawa, and stored nerve and blister agents there until 1971. Japan
signed the NPT in 1970, ratified the BWC and, in 1995, the CWC, and adopted the Three
Non-Nuclear Principles. Its large plutonium stock, reprocessing and rocket industry
make it a textbook case of nuclear latency, sheltered by the US nuclear umbrella. In
1994-95 the Aum Shinrikyo cult carried out sarin attacks in Matsumoto and on the Tokyo
subway.

narrative: Kazakhstan bore the brunt of Soviet nuclear testing and then, as an independent state,
became one of the most committed champions of disarmament. From 1949 to 1989 the
Semipalatinsk test site in the Kazakh steppe hosted 456 nuclear explosions, including
116 atmospheric tests before 1963, with little regard for the people living nearby;
studies have since found sharply higher cancer and mortality rates in exposed
villages. Public anger, mobilised from 1989 by the Nevada-Semipalatinsk movement led
by the poet Olzhas Suleimenov, helped force the last test that year and the site's
closure on 29 August 1991. When Kazakhstan declared independence in December 1991, it
inherited the world's fourth-largest arsenal: about 1,400 warheads on SS-18
intercontinental missiles, together with 40 Tu-95 bombers carrying cruise missiles,
though operational command stayed with the Russian forces in Moscow. The Soviet Union
had also built on Kazakh soil the only Biopreparat biological weapons plant outside
Russia, at Stepnogorsk, and a chemical plant at Pavlodar that never produced agents.
Kazakhstan chose rapid denuclearisation with US help: it acceded to the NPT in 1993,
returned all its warheads to Russia by the mid-1990s, and in 1994 let the United
States airlift 581 kg of highly enriched uranium out of the country under Project
Sapphire. A 26-year joint project with the US Defense Threat Reduction Agency sealed
the test tunnels and boreholes, with the last infrastructure blown up in 2000.
Kazakhstan ratified the CTBT in 2002, helped create the 2006 Central Asian
nuclear-weapon-free zone, hosts the IAEA's low-enriched uranium fuel bank, opened in
2019, and is the only former Soviet state to have ratified the TPNW. It is also the
world's largest uranium producer, with about 41% of global supply, a scale of activity
that some analysts see as a lingering proliferation risk even though Kazakhstan has
kept a clean record under the NPT.

narrative: Libya under Muammar Gaddafi pursued nuclear, chemical and missile programs from his
seizure of power in 1969 until December 2003, when he announced that Libya would give
them all up. His nuclear ambitions were open: in 1970 he tried, and failed, to
persuade Zhou Enlai to sell China's bomb, citing Israel's arsenal as his reason, and
Libya later sought uranium, conversion plants and expertise from Belgium, Japan, India
and the Soviet Union, which built the Tajoura research reactor in the 1980s. From 1985
Libya relied on a smuggling network with links to Pakistan and, investigators found,
to Chinese bomb designs. A Swiss engineer led its centrifuge effort, but even after
receiving parts in 1997 Libya could not run more than a single machine and told the
IAEA it lacked the experts to proceed. Gaddafi offered to trade the programs for an
end to sanctions from the late 1990s and finally did so in 2003, after the US invasion
of Iraq; American, British and IAEA teams removed the equipment, and the rollback
exposed the Khan network. Chemical weapons were more advanced. Libya secretly acquired
a capability from the Soviet Union in 1970, built production plants in the 1980s, and
was accused by Chad of chemical use in 1987. On joining the Chemical Weapons
Convention in 2004 it declared 24.7 tonnes of mustard agent, 1,390 tonnes of
ingredients for sarin and 3,563 empty aerial bombs. Destruction halted when the 2011
uprising began, after which rebels found an undeclared mustard stock at Jufra; the
remaining mustard munitions were destroyed with US help in 2014 and the last chemical
ingredients, shipped to Germany, by November 2017. Gaddafi's Scud missiles, fired in
the 2011 civil war, were destroyed by NATO strikes. Libya ratified the Biological
Weapons Convention in 1982 and signed the TPNW in 2017.

narrative: Mexico is a capable nuclear state that chose early and firmly to forgo the bomb, and
it has been one of the leading voices for disarmament ever since. Its use of radiation
goes back to X-rays in the late nineteenth century and medical radioisotopes from the
1920s, and nuclear science became a formal field of study in the late 1940s. A
national nuclear energy committee ran programs ranging from physics and reactors to
agronomy, genetics and radiological protection, and in 1964 it began building the
Salazar Nuclear Center in the State of Mexico, which gained a particle accelerator in
1966 and a TRIGA Mark III research reactor in 1968; in 1972 the committee became the
National Institute for Nuclear Research. In the 1970s the institute produced highly
enriched uranium, and the article notes that Mexico has the technical capability to
make nuclear weapons. Politically, it moved the other way. In 1961 the government
argued that the use of nuclear weapons could never be justified as self-defence under
the UN Charter, and Mexico was central to the Treaty of Tlatelolco, under which Latin
American states agreed not to manufacture nuclear weapons and to use nuclear
technology only for peaceful ends. In 2000 it was one of seven countries to launch the
New Agenda declaration calling for full implementation of the NPT's disarmament
provisions. In April 2010 it agreed to give up its highly enriched uranium, with US
help converting the material at its research facilities into a form unusable for
weapons; by March 2012 all of it had been removed. Mexico's Laguna Verde power station
now runs on low-enriched fuel bought from Russia's Rosatom, and in 2012 Mexico joined
the Nuclear Suppliers Group as an observer. It signed the TPNW in 2017 and ratified it
in January 2018. The article does not cover chemical or biological weapons.

narrative: Myanmar is a case of smoke without confirmed fire: for three decades it has been
accused of seeking nuclear and chemical weapons, and in each case the evidence has
stayed contested. The nuclear story begins with a controversial 2007 agreement with
Russia for a research centre with a 10 MW reactor fuelled by 20% enriched uranium. In
August 2009 the Sydney Morning Herald, citing two high-ranking defectors in Australia,
reported that the junta aimed to build a weapon by 2014 with North Korean help,
including a reactor and plutonium facilities in tunnels near Naung Laing in Mandalay
division. In June 2010 the exile broadcaster Democratic Voice of Burma published
documents smuggled out by a former army major, Sai Thein Win, and a UN report said
North Korea had been exporting nuclear technology to Myanmar, Iran and Syria. The
former inspector Robert Kelley concluded that Myanmar intended to go nuclear but was
far from succeeding; others, including the Institute for Science and International
Security, noted that the equipment shown could also serve rare-earth or titanium
production. Washington voiced concern about NPT compliance in 2011, and by 2012 said
its concerns had been partially allayed. The chemical allegations are older. In 1991
US Naval Intelligence listed Burma among states that probably possessed chemical
weapons, but the United States dropped it from that list in 1993. In 2005 army
deserters described handling chemical shells and a British physician reported injuries
among Karenni rebels consistent with chemical attack; the government denied it, and
the Nuclear Threat Initiative judged riot control agents the likelier explanation and
found no evidence of a program. In 2014 a magazine reported a chemical weapons factory
in Magway Region, and its editor and four journalists were jailed for ten years.

American nuclear weapons since 1960 and trains its pilots to deliver them. From the
1960s to the 1990s Dutch artillery and missile units were assigned US nuclear shells
and warheads for Honest John and later Lance missiles, stored at 't Harde and
Havelterberg; all are long retired. Until 2006 Royal Netherlands Navy maritime patrol
aircraft, first P-2 Neptunes and then P-3 Orions flying from Valkenburg and Curacao,
were assigned US nuclear depth bombs for anti-submarine warfare, kept under US Marine
guard at RAF St Mawgan in Cornwall under a 1965 US-British arrangement. The current
mission is at Volkel Air Base, where the US Air Force was reported in 2008 to hold 22
B61 bombs for use by Dutch aircraft, now F-35s; the infobox puts the present number at
10 to 22. Successive governments have neither confirmed nor denied the weapons, but
two former prime ministers, Dries van Agt and Ruud Lubbers, acknowledged them in 2013.

to go to war, so that no transfer breaches the NPT, a reading other states dispute.

national research organisation TNO had tested sarin, tabun, soman and a modified

only in joint trials with France and Belgium in Algeria. Dutch companies were among
those that sold Iraq chemicals later used against Iran. The Netherlands ratified the
Geneva Protocol in 1930, the BWC in 1972, the NPT in 1975 and the CWC in 1995.

narrative: North Korea showed interest in nuclear weapons in the 1950s, and its program is traced
to 1962. The Soviet Union, and later China, refused to help build a bomb, but Moscow
supplied a research reactor at Yongbyon in the 1960s. North Korea joined the NPT in
1985 but resisted inspections; when the IAEA found its declaration incomplete in 1993
it announced withdrawal, a crisis eased by the 1994 Agreed Framework, which froze its
reactor program in return for promised power reactors. The deal collapsed in 2002-03
amid US charges of a secret uranium program, and North Korea expelled inspectors and
became the only state to announce withdrawal from the NPT. Pakistan later acknowledged
that A.Q. Khan had passed it nuclear technology. Six-party talks ran until 2007
without lasting results. North Korea tested a nuclear device in October 2006, the
first of six tests at Punggye-ri, ending in September 2017 with a claimed hydrogen
bomb roughly ten times more powerful than its earlier tests. That year it also flew
ICBMs able to reach the continental United States. Laws in 2022 and 2023 declared it a
nuclear state, wrote the program into the constitution and provided for automatic
nuclear retaliation if its leadership is attacked, and in 2024 it signed a strategic
partnership treaty with Russia. It is estimated to hold about 60 warheads in 2025,
with some South Korean estimates far higher, alongside more than 360 ballistic
missiles and new cruise missiles. North Korea is also believed to hold one of the
world's largest chemical arsenals, 2,500 to 5,000 tonnes, and suspected North Korean
agents used VX to kill Kim Jong-nam in Malaysia in 2017. It has never joined the CWC;
it is a BWC party, though whether it has an offensive biological program is unclear.

Al Kibar reactor.

narrative: Pakistan kept to a non-nuclear policy until its defeat in the 1971 war with India. At
a meeting in Multan in January 1972, Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto launched a
weapons program, famously saying Pakistanis would go hungry if that was the price of a
bomb, and India's 1974 test added urgency. Two bodies led the work: the Pakistan
Atomic Energy Commission and the laboratories at Kahuta under Abdul Qadeer Khan, who
brought expertise from the European firm Urenco and built a clandestine procurement
network; a Dutch court convicted him in absentia in 1983, a verdict later overturned
on a technicality. Saudi Arabia and Libya supplied money, and the United States
alleged major Chinese help, which China denies. Pakistan carried out its first cold,
non-explosive test in 1983, and Khan later claimed a usable bomb by 1984, but it
tested openly only in May 1998, when the Chagai-I and Chagai-II series answered
India's tests within weeks. The two rivals agreed a testing moratorium in the 1999
Lahore Declaration. Khan's network later passed nuclear technology to Libya, North
Korea and Iran. Pakistan's arsenal is estimated at about 170 warheads in 2025, carried
by roughly 126 land-based missiles with ranges up to about 2,750 km and by Mirage
fighters with bombs and Ra'ad cruise missiles; a submarine-launched cruise missile is
in development. Its doctrine rejects no first use and relies on small battlefield
weapons to offset India's conventional strength. Pakistan remains outside the NPT and
the CTBT and has blocked talks on a fissile material cutoff treaty. Decisions rest
with the National Command Authority; US and other foreign experts have long questioned
the arsenal's security, which Pakistan firmly rejects. Pakistan is a party to the BWC
and the CWC and is not known to have chemical or biological weapons programs.

constitution explicitly forbids nuclear weapons on its soil, but for twenty years it
was a major American storage site. From December 1957 the United States kept hundreds
of nuclear weapons in the Philippines: gravity and depth bombs, and tactical weapons
such as Falcon air-to-air missiles, ASROC anti-submarine missiles and Talos
surface-to-air missiles. A US document from 1969 says President Ferdinand Marcos was
told of them in 1966, but that public knowledge would gravely damage relations; the
weapons were revealed only much later. When US weapons left Taiwan in 1974 they went
to Clark Air Base, and by 1977 at the latest none remained. The country's own nuclear
history is civilian. The Philippine Atomic Energy Commission dates from 1958, and
after declaring martial law Marcos announced in 1973 a power plant at Bataan, citing
the oil crisis. It was finished in 1984, but in 1986, after Marcos's fall and the
Chernobyl disaster, President Corazon Aquino chose not to run it, given its nearness
to a fault line and to Mount Pinatubo. In 2016 former defence secretary Juan Ponce
Enrile claimed the plant had a secondary weapons purpose that could have deterred
China, though he admitted he was no expert; he repeated the call in 2019, and the
defence secretary replied that the Philippines had neither the capability nor the
legal freedom, as an NPT party. President Benigno Aquino III had also rejected the
idea. The Philippines ratified the TPNW in 2021, is a ratifier of the BWC and a
signatory of the Southeast Asian nuclear-weapon-free zone treaty, signed the CWC in
1993, and in 2025 passed a law banning chemical weapons. In 2024 police seized up to
85 kg of illegally stored uranium from a smuggling ring.

narrative: Rhodesia is one of the few states known to have actually used chemical and biological
agents, a small and rudimentary effort waged during the last years of the Rhodesian
Bush War against a growing nationalist insurgency. The program grew out of the
worsening security situation after neighbouring Mozambique became independent in 1975.
It was proposed by Robert Symington, a professor at the University of Rhodesia's
medical school, through Defence Minister P. K. van der Byl to Prime Minister Ian Smith
and his war cabinet, which handed it to the Central Intelligence Organisation; the
Special Branch element of the Selous Scouts carried it out. Experiments and operations
began at the Selous Scouts base at Bindura in 1976, and from 1978 the most sensitive
work, including experiments on humans, almost certainly moved to a more remote site at
Mount Darwin. Participants confirmed the program's existence and said it ran until
late 1979. The agents were mostly cheap, locally available pesticides and poisons
rather than military agents, with some biological agents, and the aim was to kill
guerrillas inside Rhodesia and in their camps in Mozambique, and to sow distrust
between guerrillas and the villagers who supported them. The CIO chief, police
commissioners and the combined operations command were all briefed, though how far the
political leadership was involved is unclear for lack of records and witnesses. At
times the effort killed more insurgents than conventional units did: at least 809
deaths were recorded, and the true total was almost certainly over 1,000, yet it had
no meaningful effect on the war's outcome. Some writers also blame Rhodesia for an
anthrax outbreak from 1978 to 1984 that caused about 200 deaths, a claim others reject
for lack of evidence. Rhodesia had no nuclear program, and in April 1980 the former
colony became independent Zimbabwe.

campaigning against the arms race. Its nuclear research began in 1949 with isotopes
for medicine and industry, and between 1952 and 1960 Romania delivered 17,288 tons of
uranium ore to the Soviet Union for its weapons effort. Some scholars date a military
interest to 1967, as Romania played Britain, France, the United States and others off
against each other for reactor deals on easier terms. Romania ratified the NPT in
1970, but in 1978 it began the Danube Program at the Atomic Physics Institute in
Magurele, under Securitate supervision; according to its former director, Mihai
Balanescu, it had departments for nuclear weapons, for medium-range missiles and for
chemical and biological weapons. One account links the 1978 defection of Securitate
general Ion Mihai Pacepa to an order to obtain bomb technology, and a former head of
the nuclear waste agency later claimed Romania held 26 kg of plutonium in the 1980s.

December 1981, and in 1989 said Romania had the technology for the bomb but was
resolved to fight nuclear weapons; that July Hungary accused it of nuclear and missile
threats, which Bucharest denied. Its Scud-B and Luna missiles carried conventional
warheads, since Soviet nuclear warheads would be supplied only in wartime. After the
1989 revolution the program ended. Romania declared to the IAEA about 100 mg of
plutonium separated in 1985, opened its facilities to inspection, and later returned
enriched uranium to the IAEA, Russia and the United States; it also emerged that it
had diverted 14 tonnes of heavy water to India in 1986, a further NPT breach. In 2016

narrative: Soviet era (to 1991): The Soviet atomic project began in 1942 at the urging of the
physicist Georgy Flyorov, was accelerated after Hiroshima, and drew heavily on
espionage inside the Manhattan Project. Its first test, at Semipalatinsk in August
1949, opened the arms race; a true two-stage thermonuclear test followed in 1955 and,
in 1961, the Tsar Bomba, the most powerful explosion ever produced. The USSR conducted
715 tests before stopping in 1990. Its arsenal peaked at about 45,000 warheads in the
mid-1980s, spread across a full triad and some 11,000 tactical weapons, and Soviet
warheads were stationed in East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Poland and Mongolia,
and briefly in Cuba during the 1962 crisis. In 1969 Moscow weighed a massive nuclear
strike on China. The 1957 Kyshtym disaster remains the worst military nuclear accident
on record. The Soviet Union also built the largest chemical and biological programs in
history. Through the civilian front Biopreparat it ran 40 to 50 facilities employing
up to 65,000 people, in breach of the BWC it ratified in 1975; the 1979 Sverdlovsk
anthrax leak, which killed dozens, and later defectors such as Ken Alibek exposed the
effort. The chemical program produced sarin, soman, VR, mustard, lewisite and the
Novichok family. Russian Federation era (1991 on): Russia took over the Soviet arsenal
and treaty seat as continuator state. Tactical warheads in other republics came home
by May 1992, and under the Lisbon Protocol and Budapest Memorandum the strategic
warheads in Belarus, Ukraine and Kazakhstan followed by 1996. Russia declared 39,967
tons of chemical weapons under the CWC and, after missed deadlines, the OPCW confirmed
their destruction in 2017; yet Novichok was used against Sergei Skripal in 2018 and
Alexei Navalny in 2020, attacks Russia denies, and its forces have admitted dropping
CS gas in Ukraine. The US State Department assesses that an offensive biological
program continues. Russia now holds the world's largest nuclear arsenal, about 4,400
stockpiled warheads in 2026 with roughly 1,794 deployed, plus the largest tactical
arsenal, and extends a nuclear umbrella to CSTO members. Since invading Ukraine in
2022 it has made repeated nuclear threats, suspended New START in 2023 before the
treaty lapsed in 2026, withdrawn its CTBT ratification, stationed nuclear-capable
systems in Belarus, and in 2024 broadened the conditions for first use. The 2006
polonium poisoning of Alexander Litvinenko is described as a radiological attack.

narrative: Singapore has never had weapons of mass destruction of its own, but in the 1960s it
was Britain's nuclear base east of Suez, and in the Second World War it hosted part of

Unit 9420, a branch of Unit 731, set up its headquarters and laboratories at the King
Edward VII College of Medicine and nearby buildings, researching plague, cholera,
smallpox, anthrax and other diseases, and the Malay Peninsula became the army's
largest flea-breeding site outside Japan and China; one historian suspects human
experiments as well. After the war Singapore became central to British strategy in the
Southeast Asia Treaty Organization. A 1956 report to the Chiefs of Staff concluded
that nuclear weapons would have to be used in any war between SEATO and China, with
bombing aimed at airbases in North Vietnam and southern China, and Harold Macmillan

narrative: Spain's entry in the navbox is Project Islero, the Franco-era attempt to build a
nuclear weapon, and the article covers nothing else. Spain's nuclear institutions
began in secret: in 1948 Franco created a Board for Nuclear Research by decree, made
public in 1951 as the Nuclear Energy Board, and the 1955 Atoms for Peace agreement
with the United States opened the way to research reactors. After the 1957-58 Ifni War
with Morocco, the Defence High Command began to think about armed deterrence, and in
1963 General Agustin Munoz Grandes, who wanted Spain independent of NATO and
Washington, launched the project under the air force general and physicist Guillermo
Velarde. The 1966 Palomares crash of a US B-52 carrying four hydrogen bombs gave
Spanish technicians a chance to study the debris, but later that year Franco halted
physical work, fearing sanctions, while letting research continue, and kept Spain out
of the NPT. Spain produced its first plutonium outside IAEA control in 1969. In 1971
the project resumed with French support, since de Gaulle and Pompidou saw an atomic
Spain as a counterweight to the United States, and the Vandellos reactor opened in
1972. In December 1973 Velarde reported that Spain could make three bombs a year;
Prime Minister Carrero Blanco showed the report to Henry Kissinger, and was
assassinated the next morning, an event some scholars have linked, without proof, to
the CIA. Franco then stopped the military effort, judging that a small arsenal was not
worth a US blockade, but the work lingered under later governments, alarming
Washington when the Soria research centre's capacity became known in 1977. Under the
Carter campaign against NPT holdouts, Spain accepted IAEA inspection in February 1981,
and it signed the NPT in October 1987 under Felipe Gonzalez. The article does not
cover chemical or biological weapons.

Hiroshima and Nagasaki, as part of a postwar decision to stay neutral while being able
to defend itself against any invader, above all the Soviet Union. In 1948 the defence
research institute FOA presented the first concrete plans for an atomic weapon, and a
civilian nuclear power program was designed alongside it, using domestic uranium, so
that the Agesta and Marviken reactors could produce plutonium for bombs while
generating electricity. The plan called for 100 warheads over ten years, to be carried
by a planned Saab 36 attack aircraft and later by submarines and other aircraft.

climate turned the decision. By the end of the decade the government reportedly had to
choose between a bomb and a new fighter, the Saab 37 Viggen, and chose the fighter.

NPT, and the last remnant, FOA's plutonium experiments, ended in 1972. Sweden kept a
civilian nuclear industry, with ten reactors in 2012, and that year sent 3.3 kg of
plutonium to the United States under a threat-reduction program. Its chemical record
is smaller. After the First World War Sweden began research, and in the 1930s it
started its first program on mustard gas; work paused in 1940, but by the end of the
Second World War new mustard and sarin programs were a military priority. Criticism
grew in the 1960s, and in 1970 the government declared it would not further develop or
produce chemical weapons. Sweden signed the CWC in 1994 and ratified the BWC in 1976.

until the Soviet invasion of Hungary in 1956 and the arms race of the 1950s gave the
idea new force. A secret commission on acquiring nuclear arms met from March 1957, and
in July 1958 the Federal Council declared that if its neighbours armed themselves,
Switzerland would have to do likewise. Voters twice rejected anti-nuclear initiatives,
in 1962 and 1963. By 1964 the military staff had drawn up cost estimates and a
recommended arsenal of bombs, artillery shells and rockets, with tests planned in
remote parts of the country and Mirage III aircraft able to reach Moscow; strategists
even contemplated use against an invader on Swiss soil. Switzerland bought uranium,
some of it held outside international safeguards until 1981, but defence budget
shortfalls and the 1969 Lucens reactor accident sapped support. It signed the NPT in

the last committee was dissolved at the end of 1988. In 2016 it sent its 20 kg of
separated plutonium, which was not weapons-grade, to the United States for disposal.

narrative: Ba'athist Syria built the Middle East's most heavily used chemical arsenal and tried,
covertly, to build a plutonium route to the bomb. It first acquired chemical weapons
from Egypt in 1973, as a deterrent against Israel on the eve of the Yom Kippur War,
and began producing its own in the mid-1980s with Soviet and other foreign help; a
former Syrian diplomat wrote that Israel's nuclear weapons were the main motive. Syria
never admitted the arsenal until July 2012, when it implied that the weapons were
reserved for foreign enemies. In the civil war that followed, government forces
carried out hundreds of attacks, chiefly with sarin and chlorine. The August 2013
Ghouta sarin attack, the deadliest, led to a US-Russian deal under which Syria joined
the Chemical Weapons Convention; the OPCW counted about 1,300 tonnes, and the declared
stockpile left the country by June 2014. Later disclosures of a ricin program and
further sites undermined that result, and an OPCW-UN inquiry blamed the Syrian
military for the 2017 Khan Shaykhun attack, which drew a US missile strike; the 2018
Douma chlorine attack brought joint US, UK and French strikes. On the nuclear side,
Syria, an NPT party, built an undeclared reactor at Al Kibar under North Korean
supervision, reportedly with Iranian coordination. Israel destroyed it in September
2007, before it was finished, and in 2011 the IAEA judged it 'very likely' a reactor
and reported Syria's non-compliance to the Security Council. After Assad fell in
December 2024, the caretaker government let inspectors into the sites, a US-brokered

September 2026 the agency confirmed an unfinished reactor and about 73 tonnes of
undeclared natural uranium. Days later the OPCW verified the first destruction of
Syrian chemical munitions since 2014. Syria is generally considered not to have had

itself had stationed nuclear weapons on the island from 1958, during the Second Taiwan
Strait Crisis, keeping some at Tainan air base until Nixon ordered them out in 1972;
the last left in 1974. China's first nuclear test in 1964 prompted Taiwan's own
effort, and in 1967 a secret program began at the Institute of Nuclear Energy Research
under the Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology, using a Canadian research
reactor, US-supplied material and uranium bought from South Africa, all nominally for
civilian power. In 1976, after the IAEA found evidence of work toward weapons-grade
plutonium, Taiwan agreed under US pressure to dismantle the program. It did not stop.

simulation, since a test was impossible on a small, crowded island, and planners
turned to the Ching-kuo fighter as a carrier after the Sky Horse missile was cancelled

and secretly a CIA source, defected with documents; a later study judged Taiwan one or

then Taiwan has been a threshold state: President Lee Teng-hui floated reviving the

nuclear weapons since 1959 and its leaders have lately hinted that this may not be the
last word. In 1961 the United States deployed Jupiter intermediate-range missiles in

in Turkey have been at Incirlik, where an estimated 20 to 30 B61 bombs were stored in

base or delivered by Turkish F-16s. Strained relations under President Erdogan,
including the 2016 coup attempt and Turkey's role in Syria, led US officials to debate
withdrawing them. Turkish rhetoric has meanwhile shifted. In September 2019 Erdogan
said he did not accept that others could have nuclear-tipped missiles while Turkey
could not, pointing to Israel, and added that work on the matter was under way. In
February 2026 Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan warned that an Iranian bomb could set off a

narrative: Ukraine came out of the Soviet collapse holding the world's third-largest nuclear
arsenal and gave it up within three years, a decision that has become one of the most
debated in nonproliferation. When the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, about one third
of its nuclear forces were on Ukrainian territory: some 130 UR-100N missiles with six
warheads each, 46 RT-23 missiles with ten, and 33 heavy bombers, about 1,700 strategic

production know-how. Ukraine's 1990 sovereignty declaration had already pledged a
non-nuclear future, but control was contested. Its armed forces took over the bomber
crews and munitions units, and in July 1993 parliament claimed ownership of the
weapons, while Moscow kept operational control of the missiles through its permissive
action links. Under the December 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Ukraine agreed to send the
warheads to Russia and joined the NPT as a non-nuclear state, in exchange for
compensation and assurances from Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom to
respect its borders and independence; France and China gave weaker pledges. With over

narrative: The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which dissolved in 1992, made two
attempts at nuclear weapons and built a chemical arsenal, though its article is brief.
Nuclear work began in 1947, when the physicist Pavle Savic was charged with a state
program and put in charge of the Institute for Physics, renamed the Vinca Nuclear
Institute a year later. The Soviet Union helped found it and sent scientists in early
1948, and a CIA report released in 2001 suggested the institute housed facilities
relevant to weapons, such as reactors and isotope separation, not just civilian
research. After the Tito-Stalin split later in 1948 Moscow cut off funding, and
Yugoslavia continued alone; the article states that weapons production was one aim of
this research. In the early 1950s, amid fears of Soviet invasion during the Informbiro
period, Tito launched a weapons program from scratch, seeing deterrence as the
guarantee of the country's sovereignty and status. It shut down after Yugoslavia
signed the NPT. A second program began after India's nuclear test of May 1974 and
ended in 1987, but Yugoslavia, and later Serbia, kept highly enriched uranium until
2010, when it was handed to Russia. Before the breakup, Yugoslavia also developed and
stored chemical weapons, including mustard gas, prepared at the Prva Iskra factory in
Baric, sarin and other blister agents; the article does not say what became of them,
and the root WMD article's 2021 table lists Serbia and Montenegro as a probable
possessor. Unattributed claims hold that Yugoslavia worked with Libya and Iraq on
missiles that could carry weapons of mass destruction, and that the Yugoslav Army used
chemical weapons against Bosnian and Croat forces during the Yugoslav Wars, but no
such use was confirmed. Serbia is the only successor state with a missile program. The
article does not cover biological weapons.
